output.rationale: This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (along with PM10) exposure and respiratory hospital admissions using distributed lag non-linear models, which is a time-series approach. The study reports quantitative associations and risk estimates for respiratory diseases including asthma and COPD. While the focus includes COVID-19 period comparisons, the core analysis meets inclusion criteria by examining PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization associations with effect estimates.

The study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory ED visits (asthma exacerbations) using what appears to be a time-series design (mixed-effects quasi-Poisson regression with daily data). However, the abstract does not explicitly report a relative risk, odds ratio, or equivalent effect measure with confidence interval. It only mentions statistical significance (P<10-4) and describes a non-linear sigmoid relationship. Without confirmation that quantitative effect estimates with CIs are reported in the full text, the decision remains uncertain.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) includes PM2.5 as exposure, (3) outcome is asthma hospitalization which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) uses case-crossover design (time-stratified), (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (0.31% increase per 1-μg/m3 PM2.5, 95% CI 0.24-0.37%), and (6) published in English. Although it examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed and reported.

This is an original case-crossover study examining the association between PM2.5 (as the primary component of AQI) and respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits for childhood asthma. The study reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Although the primary exposure is AQI, the abstract explicitly states that PM2.5 was the primary pollutant responsible for the AQI (62% of days) and that the association was strongest for PM2.5-specific AQI. The outcome is respiratory (asthma) hospitalizations and ED visits, meeting inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations (32 respiratory discharge diagnoses), (4) the study reports quantitative associations between PM2.5 and outcomes with effect estimates (positive associations reported for 31 of 32 respiratory outcomes), and (5) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly includes respiratory hospitalizations as a major outcome category.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis with DLNM; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is hospital admissions for respiratory disease; (4) the study design is time-series; (5) it reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR=1.030, 95% CI: 1.012-1.049 for PM2.5); and (6) the article is published in English. Although multiple air pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported with quantitative effect estimates.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome includes both respiratory ED presentations and hospitalizations for bronchiolitis, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with quantitative effect estimates (>10% increased risk for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. While multiple pollutants are examined (NO2, PM10, PM2.5), PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures examined, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (acute upper respiratory infections), (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) reports relative risk with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 (RR=1.0247, 95% CI: 1.0092-1.0405), and (6) published in English. Although it examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations and emergency department visits, (4) study design is case-crossover as explicitly stated, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the population is specific (childhood cancer survivors), this does not violate any exclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure (along with PM10 and NO2), reports respiratory hospitalizations (bronchiolitis) as the outcome, and provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. The study is published in English and reports quantitative effect estimates for PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, (2) exposure includes PM2.5 (fine particulate matter), (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) study design is case-crossover, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., OR=1.004 [0.955-1.056] overall and stratified estimates), and (6) appears to be published in English. The study examines effect modification by particle constituents but still reports PM2.5 mass concentration associations.

While this study meets several inclusion criteria (time-series design, PM2.5 exposure, reports RR with effect estimates, original research), the outcome is hospitalization specifically for SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 infection rather than general respiratory hospitalizations. COVID-19 hospitalizations represent a specific infectious disease outcome that differs from the broader category of respiratory hospitalizations typically examined in PM2.5 systematic reviews. The review appears to focus on general respiratory hospitalizations, not disease-specific infectious outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) outcome is asthma emergency department visits (respiratory ED visits), (4) time-series study design clearly stated, (5) reports rate ratios with 95% credible intervals (e.g., RR=1.016, 95% CI: 1.008-1.025 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Asthma ED visits are a specific type of respiratory emergency department visit, which falls within the scope of respiratory hospitalization/ED visit outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include both respiratory ED presentations and hospital admissions, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports incidence rate ratios with 95% CIs (e.g., IRR 1.043, 95% CI: 1.000-1.089 for ED presentations), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalizations, (4) the study design is time-series, (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported (e.g., increased risk percentages and relative risk mentioned), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants and temperature, PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalizations, (4) time-series analysis with GAM was used, (5) the results indicate that effect estimates (increased risks) were calculated for the association between PM2.5 and RD hospitalizations, and (6) the article is published in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state the numerical effect estimates with confidence intervals, it clearly states that PM2.5 exposures were associated with increased risks of hospitalizations, which indicates quantitative effect measures were reported in the full text.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (wildfire smoke PM2.5), (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (acute respiratory infections, pneumonia, COPD, asthma, and other respiratory diseases), (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports relative risk with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly includes respiratory hospitalizations as a primary outcome.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using generalized additive Poisson model, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (hospital admissions for URTI), (4) time-series design analyzing daily data, (5) reports quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (0.84% increase per 10 μg/m³, 95% CI 0.05-1.64%), and (6) published in English. Upper respiratory tract infections are respiratory conditions requiring hospitalization.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations for asthma and COPD. It reports quantitative risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 exposure. Although the main finding was for NO2, PM2.5 was explicitly analyzed and reported with effect estimates (RR for asthma: 0.981-1.148; RR for COPD: 0.966-1.019). The study meets all inclusion criteria.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, quantitative effect estimates with CI, English language), it fails the study design criterion. The abstract explicitly states this is a 'retrospective cohort study' using distributed lag models, not a time-series or case-crossover design as required by the inclusion criteria.

While this is an original epidemiological study with PM2.5 exposure (from wildfire smoke), time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary outcomes are cardiovascular and cerebrovascular ED visits, not respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits. Although respiratory conditions are mentioned as a secondary finding, the study's focus and design are centered on cardiovascular/cerebrovascular outcomes, making it inappropriate for a systematic review specifically on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory ED visits (pneumonia, COPD/asthma). It uses a time-series design with distributed lag models and quasi-Poisson regression. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI) for respiratory outcomes including pneumonia. Although it also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it meets all inclusion criteria for the respiratory component.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory (pneumonia) hospitalizations with quantitative effect estimates, it uses a prospective cohort design rather than the required time-series or case-crossover design. The inclusion criteria specifically limit eligible study designs to time-series or case-crossover studies only.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory emergency room visits using a generalized additive model (consistent with time-series design). It reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR = 1.011, 95%CI: 1.002, 1.020). The outcome is respiratory emergency department visits, which meets the inclusion criteria for respiratory hospitalization/ED visits. The study analyzes both total PM2.5 and source-specific PM2.5, making PM2.5 a primary exposure of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure among multiple pollutants, (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) case-crossover design is clearly stated, (5) reports percentage change in odds with 95% CI (equivalent to OR), and (6) published in English. The study reports a 1.2% increase in odds of admission per 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 with confidence intervals.

While this is an original time-series study with PM2.5 exposure and quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome is hospitalization for rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD), which is a specific autoimmune/rheumatologic condition with respiratory manifestations, not general respiratory hospitalization. The review targets respiratory hospitalizations (e.g., asthma, COPD, pneumonia, general respiratory conditions), not hospitalizations for autoimmune diseases that happen to affect the lungs.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory ED visits as outcomes (asthma/wheeze, bronchitis, pneumonia, upper respiratory infections), provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and is published in English in a peer-reviewed journal.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 exposure explicitly stated, (3) respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits for asthma and COPD, (4) time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports excess rates with 95% CI (e.g., ER = 2.1%, 95% CI = 0.7%, 3.6%), and (6) appears to be in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

While the title mentions 'hospitalization', the abstract clearly describes the outcome as 'outpatient visits' for upper respiratory tract infections, not hospitalizations or ED visits. The study uses a generalized additive model (time-series design) and examines PM2.5 exposure, but does not meet the outcome criteria of respiratory hospitalization or emergency department visit.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using Poisson regression; (2) Exposure is PM2.5; (3) Outcomes include both respiratory ED visits and hospitalizations; (4) Study design is time-series (daily counts linked with daily PM2.5 estimates); (5) Reports multiple RR estimates with 95% CIs for respiratory outcomes (e.g., RR=1.25 [1.21, 1.30] for respiratory disease EDVs); (6) Published in English. The study examines both ED visits and hospitalizations for respiratory conditions, making it highly relevant to the systematic review.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations for AECOPD. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI) for the association between PM2.5 and hospitalizations. Although the study focuses on interaction effects with temperature and includes multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, and respiratory hospitalization is the outcome. The study meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) study design is time-series regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CI (1.61% increase per 10 μg/m3, 95% CI = 0.87, 2.35%), and (6) published in English. The use of predicted rather than measured PM2.5 does not disqualify the study as it still examines the PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization association.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is source-specific PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits for influenza and pneumonia, (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) reports excess rates with 95% CIs (e.g., ER=9.2%, 95% CI: 4.3%, 14.3%), and (6) published in English. While the study examines source-specific PM2.5 rather than total PM2.5, PM2.5 is the primary exposure being analyzed.

This is an original time-series study using generalized additive models examining the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and emergency department visits for upper respiratory tract infection. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 (5.302% increase, 95% CI: 3.202, 7.445 per 10 ug/m3). URTI is a respiratory condition requiring ED visits, meeting the outcome criteria. All inclusion criteria are satisfied.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a generalized additive model, which is characteristic of time-series analysis; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalization (pneumonia and asthma) in children; (4) the study design is time-series based on the methodology described (GAM with lag structure analyzing daily hospitalization rates against air pollutant concentrations); (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (2.22% increase per 10-unit PM2.5 increase, 95%CI: 0.64%, 3.82%); and (6) the article is published in English. While multiple pollutants are analyzed, PM2.5 is specifically included and reported separately.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is asthma emergency room admissions which qualifies as respiratory ED visits, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (7.2% increase, 95% CI 1.7-13.1%), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study with case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly listed as one of the exposures assessed, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (ILD admissions are respiratory hospitalizations), (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported for multiple pollutants including the PM2.5 exposure of interest, and (6) published in English. While the abstract emphasizes SO2 and NO2 results, PM2.5 was measured and analyzed as stated in the methods.

This is a time-series study examining emergency hospital admissions for respiratory causes with PM2.5 as one of the exposures analyzed. However, the abstract does not report the specific effect estimate (RR with CI) for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations - only results for NO2, ozone, and noise are presented. PM2.5 is listed as a main independent variable in methods, but without the PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization effect estimate in the abstract, it's uncertain whether this association was analyzed and reported in the full text.

This is an original epidemiological study using time-series design (generalized additive model with distributed lag models) examining PM2.5 exposure and COPD hospitalizations. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increases in daily admissions). COPD hospitalizations are a respiratory hospitalization outcome. The study meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) it uses a case-crossover design, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (1.73% increase, 95% CI: 1.34%, 2.12% for PM2.5), and (6) it is published in English. Although it also examines PM2.5-10, PM2.5 is explicitly included as a separate exposure.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia, acute bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and asthma), (4) study design is ecological time series, (5) reports relative risk estimates with values (RR = 1.017, 1.022, 1.020 at different lags), and (6) published in English. The study uses appropriate time-series methodology with generalized additive Poisson regression and lag structures.

The study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospital admissions with quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI). However, the study design is a difference-in-differences approach with distributed lag non-linear models, which is neither a traditional time-series nor case-crossover design as specified in the inclusion criteria. While this is a valid epidemiological approach for examining short-term exposure effects using daily data across multiple regions, it does not strictly match the required study designs. The decision depends on whether the systematic review accepts alternative quasi-experimental designs or strictly requires time-series or case-crossover studies.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is emergency department visits for respiratory diseases (COPD and upper respiratory diseases), (4) uses a case-crossover study design, (5) reports positive associations (effect estimates) for PM2.5 with various lag periods, and (6) published in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state the numerical effect estimates with confidence intervals, it clearly indicates that quantitative associations were tested and positive results were found for PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (ALRI including CAP, AECB, AECOPD, AEB), (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 0.73%; 95% CI: 0.40%, 1.06% for total ALRIs per 10-μg/m3 increase in PM2.5), and (6) published in English.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and hospital admissions across multiple disease categories, including respiratory diseases. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals (e.g., percent increase in admissions per 10-μg/m3 increase in PM2.5). Although the study examines multiple outcomes beyond respiratory hospitalizations, respiratory diseases are explicitly included as one of the major disease categories analyzed, making it eligible for inclusion in the systematic review.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and asthma emergency room visits. It uses generalized additive model with Poisson regression on daily counts, reports relative risks with 95% CIs for PM2.5 effects on respiratory ED visits (asthma ERVs). Although the study also examines PM2.5-bound PAHs, it explicitly reports PM2.5 effects separately and meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) it uses a time-series design with generalized additive models, (5) it reports percentage change with 95% CI (equivalent to effect estimates), and (6) the abstract is in English. The study provides quantitative effect estimates for PM2.5 (0.755%; 95% CI: 0.422, 1.089% per 10 μg/m3 increase).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure, (3) outcome is asthma-related emergency department visits (AEDv), which are respiratory ED visits, (4) time-series design is clearly stated, (5) quantitative effect estimates (RR with percent increase) are reported for PM2.5 (4.4% increase per IQR), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are analyzed, PM2.5 is one of them with specific effect estimates provided.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma-related hospital admissions and emergency department visits (respiratory hospitalizations), (4) case-crossover design is clearly stated, (5) the results mention positive associations and 95% confidence intervals indicating effect estimates were reported, and (6) published in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants and effect modification, PM2.5 is a primary exposure of interest.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations using a time-series design (GAM). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospital admissions (1.03% increase per 10 μg/m3, 95% CI: 0.50%-1.56%). Although the study examines multiple outcomes beyond respiratory hospitalizations, it meets all inclusion criteria for the systematic review.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other particle metrics) and hospital admissions including respiratory outcomes. While the abstract emphasizes cardiovascular results, it explicitly states that secondary pollutants including PM2.5 were important for respiratory outcomes. The study uses Poisson regression time-series analysis and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals. It examines emergency hospital admissions which meets the outcome criteria.

This is an original time-series study using GAMs that examines PM2.5 exposure and multiple health outcomes including respiratory hospitalizations. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs for respiratory system diseases (NO2: 1.36%, 95%CI: 0.74-1.98%). Although the study examines multiple pollutants and multiple disease categories, it meets all inclusion criteria: it includes PM2.5 as an exposure, respiratory hospitalizations as one of the outcomes, uses a time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization and ED visits for asthma exacerbations, (4) time-series study design using Poisson regression, (5) reports relative risk with 95% CI for PM2.5 exposure, and (6) published in English. The study specifically reports RR values for PM2.5 at different lag periods for both ED admissions and hospitalizations.

Although this is a time-series study examining respiratory ED visits with effect estimates reported, and PM2.5 was included as a covariate in the analysis, the primary exposure of interest is thunderstorm-related climate parameters (precipitation and temperature), not PM2.5. The results explicitly state that PM2.5 levels were not significantly associated with asthma ED visits on thunderstorm days, and no effect estimates for PM2.5 are reported. PM2.5 was only used as a control variable in the model, not as the main exposure being investigated.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design with generalized additive model; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (acute lower respiratory tract infections including pneumonia and bronchitis); (4) the study design is time-series; (5) relative risks with 95% confidence intervals are reported for PM2.5 (RR=1.0064, 95% CI 1.0004-1.0124 for pneumonia at lag4 and RR=1.0133, 95% CI 1.0025-1.0242 for bronchitis at lag010); and (6) the abstract is in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure (along with PM10), reports respiratory hospitalizations for asthma and COPD as outcomes, provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and appears to be published in English.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations using a time-series design with Poisson regression. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospital admissions (7.5% increase, 95% CI: 4.9-10.2% per 12.4 μg/m3 increase). All inclusion criteria are met.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) time-series study design using Poisson regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (percentage increases in hospitalization rates per 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 with specific values for overall and racial/ethnic subgroups), and (6) published in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (1.74% increase per 10-μg/m3, 95% CI: 1.41-2.07% for respiratory admissions), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (159,365 respiratory disease admissions), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CI (1.95% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5 for respiratory diseases, 95% CI 1.63-2.27%), and (6) published in English. The study examines both cardiovascular and respiratory outcomes, but respiratory hospitalizations are explicitly analyzed and reported.

While this is a time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations with effect estimates, the primary exposure is particle oxidative potential (OP), not PM2.5 mass concentration itself. The study uses PM2.5 as a carrier to express OP measures (OP per m³), but the exposure of interest and the reported associations are for oxidative potential metrics (OP(AA) and OP(GSH)), not standard PM2.5 mass concentration. This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 as the exposure.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) exposure and emergency department visits for pediatric asthma. It uses a time-series design with Poisson generalized linear models and reports rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals. All inclusion criteria are met.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using GAM for time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure, (3) respiratory disease hospitalization is the outcome, (4) the study design is time-series based on the use of GAM to estimate short-term effects, (5) quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 1.95% increase with 95% CI: 0.25, 3.67 per 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5), and (6) the article is in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (specifically asthma hospitalizations are reported), (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.35 for asthma), and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly reports respiratory hospitalization outcomes which are relevant to the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is chronic respiratory disease (CRD) hospitalizations, (4) time-series design clearly stated, (5) reports excess risks with 95% CIs for PM2.5 (2.13%, 95% CI: 0.55%, 3.74% per 10 μg/m3 increase), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 results are specifically reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory healthcare visits (which includes hospitalizations/ED visits), (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with effect estimates for PM2.5 increases, and (6) published in English. While the abstract uses the term 'healthcare visits' rather than explicitly stating 'hospitalization' or 'ED visit', respiratory healthcare encounters in this context typically refer to hospital-based care.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is hospitalization for respiratory diseases, (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (OR=1.017, 95%CI: 1.003-1.031 for PM2.5), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other exposures) and respiratory outcomes including ED visits and hospitalizations (inpatient visits) for asthma exacerbation. The study reports rate ratios with confidence intervals. Although the primary focus is on effect modification by viral infections and the main results presented are for pollen, the abstract indicates PM2.5 was analyzed and the study meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets the inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using GAM time-series analysis; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures; (3) the outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (patients with comorbid respiratory diseases); (4) the study design is time-series based on daily data; (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (7.25% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5); (6) published in English. While the population is restricted to patients with diabetes mellitus and comorbid respiratory diseases, this is still a respiratory hospitalization outcome and meets the review criteria.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, time-series design, PM2.5 exposure, reports RR with CI), the outcome is acute upper respiratory tract infections (AURTIs), which typically refers to infections of the nose, sinuses, pharynx, and larynx (common cold, pharyngitis, sinusitis). These are generally distinct from lower respiratory conditions that typically require hospitalization (pneumonia, COPD exacerbations, asthma). The systematic review focuses on respiratory hospitalizations, which conventionally refers to more severe lower respiratory conditions rather than upper respiratory tract infections.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using generalized additive models, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) the outcome is emergency department visits for asthma (a respiratory condition), (4) it uses a time-series study design as stated in the title and methods, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 6.1% increase, CI: 2.1-10.3%), and (6) the article is in English. The study examines respiratory ED visits specifically for asthma, which falls under respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations, (4) uses case time series analysis (a variant of time-series design), (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CI (1.43% increase, 95% CI: 1.34%, 1.52% for respiratory hospitalizations per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5 increment), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly reports separate results for respiratory hospitalizations which is the outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (COPD and respiratory infection), (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 1.28% increase per 10-µg/m3 for heart failure), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (source-specific fine particulate matter), (3) outcome is respiratory disease emergency department visits, (4) study design is time-series (Poisson time-series regression models), (5) the abstract indicates associations were estimated (effect measures reported), and (6) published in English in Environmental Health Perspectives. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) the outcome is pneumonia hospitalizations which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) it reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR=1.015, 95% CI: 1.010-1.021 for PM2.5), and (5) appears to be published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (total mass and constituents), (3) includes respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome, (4) uses time-series analysis design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 3.47% increase with 95% CI: 2.03, 4.94% for respiratory admissions), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations among 214 disease groups studied, (4) time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for hospital admissions per µg/m3 increase in PM2.5, and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (among other particulate matter sizes), (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increase in risk with 95% confidence intervals implied), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations, (4) study design is explicitly time-series analysis, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with credible intervals (e.g., 0.75% increase per 10 μg/m3 with 95% CI), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as one of the exposures, (3) respiratory ED visits are analyzed as outcomes (asthma, COPD, respiratory infections), (4) time-series study design, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (e.g., 7.6% increase in asthma visits per 8.2 µg/m3 PM2.5, 95% CI 5.1-10.1), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma-related ED visits which are respiratory emergency department visits, (4) time-series study design with Poisson regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 and other pollutants. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using Poisson regression on daily hospitalization counts, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) time-series design based on daily counts methodology, (5) reports excess risk percentages with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 4.1% [95% CI, 1.8-6.4] for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure along with other pollutants, (3) outcome is emergency department visits for pediatric asthma (respiratory condition), (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR IQR=1.03, 95% CI 1.02-1.04 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory emergency department visits, (4) case-crossover design as stated in title and methods, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for respiratory outcomes (asthma/wheeze, COPD, bronchitis), and (6) published in English.

This does not meet the inclusion criteria which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visit as the outcome.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (COPD admissions), (4) time-series design using Poisson regression with lag structure, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR=1.25, 95% CI=1.22-1.27), and (6) published in English. While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design), it does not report a relative risk, odds ratio, or equivalent effect measure with confidence interval. The study only reports correlation coefficients (R values) and regression coefficients from a linear model, not the standardized effect estimates (RR/OR) required for systematic review inclusion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are reported as one of the outcomes, (4) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are provided (1.14% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5 for respiratory admissions), and (5) the abstract is in English. The study examines multiple outcomes including respiratory hospitalizations, which is directly relevant to the systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (fine particulate matter <2.5 microns), (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia and asthma), (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals for multiple lag periods, and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes PM2.5 and its components, (3) outcome is respiratory emergency department visits for pneumonia, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 18.2% increase, 95% CI 8.8-28.4% for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Pneumonia is a respiratory condition and ED visits are an appropriate outcome for this review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study comparing two analytical approaches, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as an exposure with quantitative results reported, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalizations, (4) both time-series and case-crossover designs are used, (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported as percentage increases with confidence intervals for each 10 μg/m3 increment in PM2.5, and (6) the abstract is in English. The study provides specific effect estimates for PM2.5 (e.g., 6.4% and 4.5% increases in Warsaw).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) the outcome is asthma hospital admissions (a respiratory hospitalization), (4) both time-series and case-crossover designs were used, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (e.g., 30.2% increase, 95% CI: 13.4-49.6% for PM2.5), and (6) the article is in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (pneumonia), (4) uses appropriate time-series methodology with Poisson regression, and (5) reports quantitative effect estimates showing association between PM2.5 and hospitalizations with lag effects. While the abstract does not explicitly state RR/OR with confidence intervals, it clearly indicates statistical associations were found and quantitative estimates were calculated (256 fewer admissions per 10 µg/m3 decrease), which implies effect measures were derived.

COPD admissions are a respiratory hospitalization outcome. All inclusion criteria are met.

This is an original time-series study that examines PM2.5 exposure (among other PM fractions) and respiratory hospital admissions. Although the main finding for respiratory admissions was associated with PM10 and PM10-2.5 during dust intrusions, PM2.5 was analyzed as one of multiple exposures, and the study meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 exposure is explicitly measured, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (asthma readmissions), (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR = 1.082, 95% CI = 1.008-1.162 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although the outcome is hospital readmissions rather than initial admissions, readmissions are still respiratory hospitalizations and meet the outcome criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original case-crossover epidemiological study, (2) includes PM2.5 exposure (along with PM10), (3) outcome is asthma-related hospital visits which are respiratory hospitalizations, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (e.g., 1.26, 95% CI 1.22-1.30), and (6) published in English. The study examines both PM10 and PM2.5, with PM2.5 being one of the exposures analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure alongside ozone, (3) outcome is respiratory (asthma) emergency department visits, (4) uses both time-series and case-crossover designs, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (RR and OR) with 95% CIs for both pollutants, and (6) published in English. Although PM2.5 was not significantly associated with the outcome, the study still examined PM2.5 and reported effect estimates, making it eligible for inclusion in the systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study examining PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization associations, (2) exposure is source-specific PM2.5, (3) outcomes are asthma and COPD hospitalizations and ED visits, (4) uses modified time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports excess rates (ERs) with specific quantitative estimates (e.g., 0.5%-3.1%, 1.3%-1.7%, 2.1%-3.4%), and (6) appears to be in English. While the study examines source-specific PM2.5 rather than total PM2.5, PM2.5 is the primary exposure of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) outcome is hospital admissions for asthma (a respiratory hospitalization), (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports OR with 95% CI for PM2.5 (OR 1.09; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.13), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) reports quantitative effect estimates as percent increases which can be converted to relative risks, (5) appears to be published in English. The study explicitly examines PM2.5 exposure and hospital admissions for respiratory diseases using appropriate time-series methodology with Poisson regression.

Although this study examines PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) exposure and uses a time-series design with effect estimates, the outcome is acute otitis media (AOM) hospitalizations, not respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using distributed lag nonlinear models; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia, COPD, asthma); (4) the study design is time-series based on daily admissions and air pollutant data; (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported (RR with 95% CI for PM2.5 at lag 12: RR=1.068, 95% CI 1.017-1.121); and (6) the abstract is in English. The study also examines PM10, but PM2.5 is one of the multiple exposures analyzed, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This is an original case-crossover study examining the association between air pollution (including PM2.5 as one component of the AQHI) and respiratory ED visits for asthma. Although the primary exposure is the composite AQHI index, PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) is explicitly stated as one of the three pollutants included in the index. The outcome is respiratory ED visits, the design is case-crossover, and quantitative effect estimates are provided.

While this study examines respiratory ED visits and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary exposure is thunderstorms and power outages, not PM2.5. PM2.5 is only examined as a mediating/modifying factor of the thunderstorm-health relationship, not as the main exposure of interest. The study does not provide direct PM2.5 exposure-respiratory hospitalization associations that would be relevant for a systematic review on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are the primary outcome, (4) it uses a time-series design, (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported (0.9-4.5% increase per 10 units PM2.5 increase), and (6) it is published in English. The abstract clearly states effect estimates with confidence in the statistical significance.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and adult pneumonia hospital visits including ED visits. The abstract indicates effect estimates were calculated (mentions statistically significant impacts and effect estimates), though specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (ICD-9: 460-519), (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports RR with 95% CI for respiratory causes (RR=1.049, 95% CI 1.019-1.078), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it includes respiratory hospitalizations as a separate outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design with Poisson regression; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) respiratory hospital admissions are examined as an outcome; (4) the study design is time-series; (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported for multiple PM fractions and respiratory hospitalizations; (6) the article appears to be published in English. Although PM2.5 did not show significant association with respiratory diseases in the results presented, the study did analyze this relationship and PM2.5 is one of multiple exposures examined, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using ecological time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalization among other outcomes, (4) study design is explicitly time-series, (5) the abstract indicates associations were estimated (effect estimates), and (6) appears to be published in English. While the study examines multiple outcomes (mortality and hospitalizations for various causes), respiratory hospitalization is specifically mentioned as one of the outcomes analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original time-series epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations, reports relative risks (RRs) with appropriate statistical modeling, and appears to be published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly includes respiratory admissions as an outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma-related ED visits which qualifies as respiratory ED visits, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the abstract primarily reports results for other pollutants (O3, CO, NO2), PM2.5 is clearly stated as one of the exposures examined in the study.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory disease hospitalizations. All inclusion criteria are met: original research, PM2.5 exposure included, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, quantitative effect estimates with CIs provided.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 source apportionment and health outcomes, (2) exposure is PM2.5 from various sources, (3) outcome is respiratory emergency department visits for asthma, pneumonia, and acute URI, (4) study design is case-crossover, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., OR=1.022, 95% CI: 1.013, 1.031 for dust and asthma), and (6) appears to be published in English. The study meets all key inclusion criteria: original epidemiological research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and quantitative effect estimates.

This is an original time-series epidemiological study that examines PM2.5 (among other exposures) and emergency hospital admissions for respiratory diseases. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Although the primary focus is on coarse PM (PMc), the methods clearly state that PM2.5 was analyzed as part of the exposure assessment and controlled for in models, making PM2.5 one of multiple exposures analyzed. This meets inclusion criteria per the exception 'unless PM2.5 is one of multiple exposures analyzed.'

This is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design to examine the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. While the primary focus is on evaluating geo-imputation methodology, the study reports hazard ratios (effect estimates) for the PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization association. It meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, case-crossover design, and reports quantitative effect estimates (HRs).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using Poisson time-series regression, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospital admissions, (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CIs for respiratory hospitalizations, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines mortality and cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly analyzes hospital admissions due to respiratory causes including COPD and asthma, which are relevant to the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) respiratory ED visits (specifically asthma) are among the outcomes examined, (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported (OR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.03-1.23 for PM2.5 and asthma), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes and other pollutants, this does not disqualify it as PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits are clearly analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (wildfire-sourced), (3) outcome includes respiratory ED visits, (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (0.47% increase per 1 μg/m3 for respiratory diseases with CI: 0.30%, 0.64%), and (6) published in English. While the PM2.5 is specifically from wildfire sources, it is still PM2.5 exposure which meets the inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations (asthma admissions) as the outcome, provides quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (12% and 3% elevation in admissions), and appears to be published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are included as outcomes (lower respiratory tract infections and COPD), (4) case-crossover study design with time-stratified approach, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 2.8% increase for lower respiratory tract infections, 1.6% for COPD), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiac outcomes and other particle sizes, it clearly includes respiratory hospitalizations with PM2.5 exposure and provides the required effect estimates.

This is an original time-series study examining the association between short-term PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (as well as circulatory). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with credible intervals for both circulatory and respiratory outcomes. It meets all inclusion criteria: original epidemiological research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence/credible intervals.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using two-stage time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) Outcome is hospital admissions for AECOPD (acute exacerbation of COPD), which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) Study design is time-series, (5) Reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR=1.093, 95% CI 1.06-1.13 for PM2.5), and (6) Published in English. The study analyzes multiple pollutants but PM2.5 is one of them with specific effect estimates reported.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations (influenza hospital visits, ICD-10 J11). While the abstract doesn't explicitly state effect estimates with confidence intervals, the methods and results sections indicate these were calculated. The focus on interactive effects with viral exposure is a specific research question but doesn't disqualify the study from examining the PM2.5-hospitalization association.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original ecological time series study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations, and reports relative risk estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 6% increase with 95%CI: 1.4-10.8 for children; 6.8% increase with 95%CI: 0.5-13.5 for elderly).

This study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure (among other pollutants), includes respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits as outcomes (COPD mentioned specifically), uses what appears to be a time-series design based on Poisson regression for short-term impacts, and reports rate ratios with statistical significance. While the study examines multiple chronic diseases (not only respiratory), it does include COPD which is a respiratory condition with hospitalization outcomes. The study design appears to be time-series given the focus on short-term impacts and daily variations in air quality.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) respiratory hospitalization is reported as an outcome, (4) case-crossover design is clearly stated, (5) quantitative effect estimates with ranges (confidence intervals) are provided for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalization (0.19%-0.69% and 0.33%-1.1% increase in odds), and (6) the article appears to be in English. Although it is a multi-pollutant study, PM2.5 results for respiratory hospitalization are specifically reported.

This is an original time-series study using Poisson regression with DLNM to examine the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations (AECOPD). The study reports quantitative effect estimates including relative cumulative risks and percentage increases in hospitalizations per 10 μg/m3 increase in pollutants. COPD exacerbations are a respiratory hospitalization outcome. All inclusion criteria are met.

The study uses hospitalization records and assigns chronic exposure based on residential ZIP code, then follows patients for outcomes, which is characteristic of a cohort design rather than the required time-series or case-crossover approaches.

This study meets the inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome includes respiratory hospital admissions (ICD-10: J00-J99), (4) Poisson generalized linear models were used which would provide effect estimates, and (5) it appears to be a peer-reviewed publication in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state effect estimates with confidence intervals, the methodology described (Poisson GLM in a time-series framework) would generate such estimates. The study analyzes multiple pollutants including PM2.5, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and pneumonia hospitalizations (a respiratory outcome). However, the abstract does not explicitly report quantitative effect estimates (RR, OR, or equivalent with confidence intervals), only stating statistical significance (P<0.05) and positive correlations. The abstract mentions PM2.5 is analyzed alongside SO2 and PM10, which is acceptable. The critical uncertainty is whether the full paper contains the required effect estimates with confidence intervals, which cannot be determined from this abstract alone.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using generalized additive models; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly listed as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) Outcome is COPD hospital admissions, which is a respiratory hospitalization; (4) Study design is time-series based on the methodology described (GAM with lag effects, controlling for temporal trends); (5) Reports percentage change in hospital admissions per 10 µg/m³ increase, which is a quantitative effect estimate; (6) Published in English. COPD hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization that fits the outcome criteria.
